newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Jews remember Exodus 50 years later.
newsitem.headline: French Jews remember Exodus 50 years later.

text.p: France on Friday marked the 50th anniversary of a sea journey that crystallised world support for a Jewish state in Palestine, and provided the plot for the best-selling novel and hit film "Exodus".

French officials, Israeli ambassador Avi Pazner and Jewish groups gathered in the Mediterranean port of Sete where 4,500 European Jews, most of them survivors of Nazi death camps, set sail on July 11, 1947 for Palestine aboard the "Exodus" only to be turned away by the British in one of the greatest refugee scandals of the era .

"People just kept getting on this very old boat and the residents of Sete who were watching were convinced we were going on a suicide journey and they made the sign of the cross," said Jacques Lipchitz, one of the passengers on the Exodus.

The ill-fated boat, one of dozens used to carry Jewish refugees to Palestine after the war, became the focus of international attention when authorities of the British mandate accosted it in the high seas and turned it away.

"When we left territorial waters, the warships started chasing us and the sea was very rough. The boat had no keel because it had been built for service on the Mississippi River, so it rocked violently back and forth, and there was a collective fit of hysteria on board," Lipchitz said.
For months the Exodus was stranded at sea while countries argued over who would take the refugees. It was sent back to France, but the passengers refused to disembark.
Its next stop was Germany, where the refugees were forced off the boat and placed in internment camps for nearly a year.

"It was horrible for these people. Some of them were partisans who had fought Germany during the war and the others who had been in concentration camps felt they were going back," said ambassador Pazner, whose father was, at the time, head of the Geneva branch of the Jewish Agency which had gathered the refugees in Sete.

With world opinion up in arms over the plight of the refugees, the United Nations General Assembly voted just a few months later, on November 29, 1947, to partition Palestine into Jewish and Arab states.
But it was not until the creation of the state of Israel in May 1948 that the refugees were allowed to leave the German internment camps and return to Palestine.
"People were outraged. It made international public opinion sensitive to the refugees' plight and it's what caused the United Nations vote creating the state of Israel," he said.
The crisis was recounted in the best-selling novel by U.S. author Leon Uris and a box-office hit film starring Paul Newman and Eva Marie Saint.

At a solemn ceremony at the port where the Exodus set off on its journey, some 500 people, including witnesses and survivors of the Exodus sang the French and Israeli national anthems before releasing blue and white balloons into the sky in honour of the refugees.
